To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the generalized coherent states of the system A are Bell states of the subsystem B and the subsystem C. Generalized coherent states of a quantum system A that splits into two subsystems are the Bell states of the system.
the Bell state is a unique state of the system that is the coherent state of the Lie algebra, and that the coherent state of any Lie algebra is the Bell state.

(1) the Bell state of a quantum particle is a generalized coherent state; (2) the Bell state is unique, and it is the same for all systems with the same Lie-group symmetry; and (3) the Bell state has a simple form for the most important systems, such as spin-1/2 particles, spin-J particles, and modes of the radiation field.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a Bell state of a system A is an entangled pure state that factorizes into a direct product of subsystem states when the system is split.
a quantum system A is Bell separable if it can be split into subsystems B and D that are Bell separable.
the Bell state is the state of the system that factorizes upon its splitting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we construct a generalized Bell state for a quantum system that is invariant under the action of the group SU(2).
the Bell states for a system with Lie-group symme­try are the generalized coherent states.
the generalized coherent state of the system is the Bell state of this system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a state of a quantum mechanical system that factorizes into a direct product of the states of its subsystems is not necessarily a Bell state.

the Bell state is a unique state that possesses the symmetry of the Lie group of the quantum system and is the most general state that factorizes under splitting into the direct products of states of the constituent subsystems.
the entangled states of a system A that factorize upon splitting are unique.
